title: Europe and Japan: the slow squeeze and the sudden yank
hook:
On the first Monday of August 2024, traders in Mumbai walked in to screens that were already red. Overnight, Tokyo's Nikkei had suffered its worst day since the crash of 1987. Nothing had happened in India. No bad results, no policy shock, no scandal. Yet the Nifty fell hard at the open and India's fear gauge, the VIX, made one of its sharpest one-day jumps outside a genuine crisis.

The trigger was a small interest rate hike by the Bank of Japan at the end of July, followed by a weak American jobs report. Together they set off a stampede out of one of the most crowded trades in global finance: borrowing yen for almost nothing and investing it everywhere else. Two days later a deputy governor of the Bank of Japan, Shinichi Uchida, said the bank would not raise rates while markets were unstable. Tokyo rebounded. Within a few weeks most of the damage in India had been repaired.

That is how Japan reaches Indian markets: suddenly, mechanically, and usually briefly. Europe works the opposite way, slowly, through export orders, energy prices and, now, a tax on the carbon inside Indian steel. This chapter explains both channels and how to tell a liquidity event from real news.
short: For decades Japan had the cheapest money in the world. Investors borrowed yen and bought higher-yielding assets everywhere, and that trade unwinds all at once when the yen jumps.
A carry unwind is a liquidity event, not information. Funds sell what they can, not what is bad, and Indian large caps are easy to sell. Historically the damage in India has been sharp and short.
The Bank of Japan is now raising rates in steps after years at zero or below. Each step makes the yen trade a little less attractive and keeps the risk of another unwind alive.

Europe is a slow-moving factor: export demand for Indian IT and engineering, dear European energy that helps Indian chemicals, and the carbon border tax that raises costs for Indian steel and aluminium.
The ECB raised rates in June 2026 for the first time since 2023, blaming energy prices pushed up by the Iran war. Europe is no longer the cheap, sleepy funding market it was.

sections.heading: The cheapest money in the world, and what people did with it
sections.html:
Start with a puzzle. Why would anyone keep money in a currency that pays nothing? Japan's answer, for most of the last three decades, was that its citizens had little choice. After its property and stock bubble burst around 1990, Japan sank into years of weak growth and falling prices. The Bank of Japan cut rates to zero by the end of the decade, and in 2016 went further, below zero. Japanese bank deposits paid essentially nothing, year after year.

Now look at it from the other side. If you can borrow yen at close to zero, you can swap it into dollars and buy a US Treasury bond paying a few percent, or swap it into Mexican pesos, or Brazilian real, or Indian bonds, and pocket the difference. That gap between what you pay to borrow and what you earn is called carry, and the strategy is the carry trade. It is the financial equivalent of borrowing from a relative who never asks for interest and lending the money to a friend who pays well.

Here's the catch. You owe yen. If the yen strengthens while you hold dollars or pesos, you need more of those to repay the same yen loan. A sharp enough yen rally can wipe out years of carry in a few days. As long as the yen drifts weaker or stays still, the trade feels like free money. When it turns, it bites.

Everyone played. Hedge funds used yen funding with heavy leverage. Japanese life insurers and the giant national pension fund poured savings into foreign bonds and shares because they could not earn anything at home, which is a big reason Japan became one of the world's largest creditor nations. And ordinary Japanese savers joined in through online currency accounts, so many of them that the market nicknamed them Mrs Watanabe. Nobody knows exactly how large the yen carry trade is at any moment. That uncertainty is part of why it scares people.

sections.heading: Why carry unwinds are so violent: everyone heads for the same door
sections.html:
Picture a crowded cinema with one exit. Most of the time nobody moves. Then someone smells smoke.

A carry unwind works the same way. Something makes the yen jump: a Bank of Japan hike, a fall in US rates that narrows the gap, a scare that sends Japanese investors home. Leveraged funds start losing money on their yen loans. Their brokers ask for more collateral, which traders call a margin call. To raise cash, the funds sell whatever they can sell quickly. Then they buy yen to repay the loans, which pushes the yen up further, which triggers the next round of margin calls. The loop feeds itself until the leverage is gone.

Notice what is missing from that story: any judgement about whether the assets being sold are good. A fund that needs cash on a Monday morning does not sell its least favourite stock. It sells its most liquid one. Indian large caps, especially the big banks, IT companies and index heavyweights that foreign funds own in size, are exactly that kind of asset. They get sold not because anything changed in India but because they can be sold.

In a carry unwind, funds sell what they can, not what they should. That is why the bounce is usually as fast as the fall.

The fear shows up most clearly in volatility. India's VIX measures how much movement options traders expect over the next month, so it rises when people rush to buy protection.

[[fig:1]]

The chart shows India's VIX week by week since mid-2015. The towering spike is the pandemic crash of 2020, a real economic shock. The bump labelled carry unwind in August 2024 is far smaller, but look at its shape: a near-vertical jump and a fast return to normal. Compare it with the Ukraine invasion in 2022 and the election result day in June 2024. Each spike is a moment when the market paid up for insurance, and in most of them the premium faded within weeks. That is the signature of a liquidity event rather than a change in the Indian story.

sections.heading: Japan wakes up: the end of free money
sections.html:
For years, warnings about the carry trade felt academic because the Bank of Japan never moved. That changed under Governor Kazuo Ueda. In March 2024 the bank ended negative rates, its first hike in seventeen years, and dropped the policy of capping long-term bond yields. It raised again in July 2024, which helped set off the August stampede. Through 2025 and into 2026 it kept going, slowly. A hike in June 2026 took the policy rate to its highest level in about three decades, and Japanese government bond yields climbed to multi-decade highs as traders bet on more.

Why is Japan finally tightening? Because, after a generation, inflation came back. Wages started rising, the weak yen made imports dearer, and prices began climbing faster than the bank's target. A central bank that spent a generation fighting deflation now has the opposite problem.

For the rest of the world this matters in two ways. The first is the carry trade itself. Each hike narrows the gap between yen borrowing costs and what investors earn elsewhere, and every narrowing makes the trade a little less attractive and a little more fragile. The second is slower and possibly bigger. Japanese pension funds and insurers sent their savings abroad because home paid nothing. If Japanese bonds now pay a decent return, some of that money may come home. Japan is one of the world's largest holders of foreign bonds, so even a gradual shift nudges up yields abroad, including in the US, which in turn tightens conditions for emerging markets like India.

The practical point: each Bank of Japan meeting is a small but real tail risk for Indian markets. The bank itself knows it. After August 2024 it went out of its way to signal hikes well in advance and to avoid surprising markets. A well-telegraphed hike is a non-event. A surprise, especially combined with a US slowdown that narrows rate gaps from the other side, is the combination that produced the last unwind.

sections.heading: Europe: the slow channel
sections.html:
Europe reaches India through the real economy rather than through panics. The European Union is one of India's biggest trading partners, and Europe is the second-largest market for Indian IT services after the United States. When European banks, insurers and manufacturers are doing well, they sign outsourcing contracts and digital projects with Indian IT firms. When they are nervous, they delay them. The effect shows up in deal wins and revenue guidance a few quarters later, not in a single bad day.

The European Central Bank sets the price of money for the twenty-odd countries that use the euro, and it matters to India mostly through that demand channel and through the euro itself. After raising rates hard in 2022 and 2023 to fight inflation, it cut through 2024 and 2025 and then held steady. Then, in June 2026, with oil and gas prices pushed up by the Iran war and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, and euro area inflation back above its target, the ECB raised rates for the first time since 2023. Executive board member Isabel Schnabel had warned that the risk of inflation expectations slipping was rising. Higher European rates cool European demand, which is a mild negative for Indian exporters selling there.

There is also a positive slow story. In March 2025, under incoming chancellor Friedrich Merz, Germany changed its constitution to loosen its famous debt brake. Defence spending above a modest threshold no longer counts against borrowing limits, and a special fund of half a trillion euros was set up for infrastructure over twelve years. For a country that had been one of the world's tightest spenders, that is a regime change. Over time it means more orders for engineering goods, components and defence supplies, some of which Indian suppliers are well placed to fill. It is a modest tailwind, not a boom, and it builds over years.

sections.heading: Dear energy in Europe, a quiet tailwind for Indian chemicals
sections.html:
Before 2022, Europe's heavy industry ran on cheap Russian gas piped across the continent. Germany's chemical giants built their business models on it. Then Russia invaded Ukraine, cut gas supplies through 2022, and in September of that year the Nord Stream pipelines under the Baltic were blown apart. European gas prices hit records. Europe replaced pipeline gas with liquefied gas shipped from the US, Qatar and elsewhere, which works but costs far more.

The result was a lasting cost disadvantage. In February 2023 BASF, the world's largest chemical company, announced thousands of job cuts and the closure of several plants at its giant Ludwigshafen site, including an ammonia plant. Its chief executive, Martin Brudermüller, blamed high energy costs and slow, heavy regulation.

Why does that matter in Mumbai? Chemicals are a business where energy and feedstock are a large part of cost. When a European plant pays far more for gas than a rival in India, the Indian plant can undercut it on price for global customers, or win contracts that used to go to Europe by default. Indian specialty chemical and pharmaceutical ingredient makers that sell to European and American buyers have benefited from exactly this shift. The catch, as the China chapter explains, is that Chinese producers are chasing the same customers at even lower prices.

The Iran war has made the energy gap matter again. A large part of the world's liquefied gas, including Qatar's, has to sail through Hormuz, and Europe competes with Asia for every cargo. Higher and more uncertain European energy costs keep the relative advantage alive for Indian producers, even as they raise costs for everyone.

sections.heading: The carbon border tax: a new toll on Indian steel
sections.html:
Europe charges its own factories for every tonne of carbon dioxide they emit, through a carbon market where permits are bought and sold. That creates a problem: a European steelmaker pays for its emissions, while a rival abroad that does not could undercut it and simply move the pollution offshore. The EU's answer is the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, usually called CBAM. Importers of certain goods must pay for the carbon embedded in what they bring in, at roughly the price European producers pay, minus any carbon price already paid at home.

The first products covered are steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen and electricity. Reporting began in October 2023 without any payment. From January 2026 the definitive phase started: importers are now liable for the carbon in their 2026 imports. After a simplification package in 2025, they start buying the certificates in February 2027 and file their first annual declaration later that year. The bill for this year's shipments is real; it just arrives next year.

India is unusually exposed. Much of its steel is made in coal-fired blast furnaces, which emit more carbon per tonne than the electric furnaces common in Europe. So the carbon charge on an Indian tonne can be large relative to its price, and smaller exporters face a heavy paperwork burden: proving actual emissions plant by plant, or being charged a punitive default value. Reports early in 2026 described cancelled orders and shipments held at European ports for missing compliance details.

CBAM turns a company's carbon footprint into a line item on its export invoice.

India and the EU concluded a free trade agreement in January 2026. It gave Indian steel a larger tariff-free quota into Europe but no exemption from CBAM, only a framework for cooperation on its implementation. The winners over time will be producers with lower emissions per tonne and the systems to prove it. The losers are high-emission exporters and small mills that cannot afford the measurement.

history_title: six times the shock came from far away

history.title: The two days the yen went vertical
history.story:
Through the mid-1990s the yen weakened steadily, and borrowing it to buy higher-yielding assets became one of the most popular trades among hedge funds. Long-Term Capital Management, the fund run by John Meriwether with Nobel laureates Myron Scholes and Robert Merton among its partners, collapsed in September 1998 after Russia defaulted. As funds everywhere slashed leverage, they scrambled to repay yen loans.

In early October the yen surged against the dollar in about two days. The Bank for International Settlements later called it the sharpest move in major currencies since the early 1970s. There was no obvious trigger in Japan; it was simply everyone heading for the exit at once.
history.lesson: Carry trades unwind on positioning, not news, which is why they are so hard to see coming.

history.title: Mrs Watanabe's hedge fund
history.story:
By the mid-2000s, Japanese currency traders had noticed a new force in the market: housewives and salaried workers trading foreign currencies online from home, often with heavy leverage, buying high-yielding currencies like the Australian and New Zealand dollar with yen. The press called them Mrs Watanabe, and by some estimates they had become a big slice of Tokyo's currency trading.

In 2007 the carry trade suffered two scares: one after a sharp fall in Shanghai in February, and a bigger one as the credit crisis began that summer. Japanese retail traders lost heavily, and the yen rallied as positions were cut.
history.lesson: When a leveraged trade has become a household hobby, it is crowded, and crowded trades exit violently.

history.title: Whatever it takes
history.story:
In late 2009 Greece's new government, under George Papandreou, revealed that the country's budget deficit was far bigger than previously reported. Bond markets panicked. Greece needed a bailout in 2010, and fear spread to Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Italy. Investors began asking whether the euro itself would survive, and global funds pulled money out of riskier markets, India included.

In July 2012, at a conference in London, ECB President Mario Draghi said the bank was ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro, adding that it would be enough. He had not announced any money. Bond yields across southern Europe began falling almost immediately.
history.lesson: European crises reach India through global risk appetite, and sometimes a central banker's sentence is enough to end one.

history.title: The morning Britain voted to leave
history.story:
In June 2016, Britain voted to leave the European Union. Prime Minister David Cameron, who had called the referendum expecting to win it, announced his resignation the next morning. The pound crashed to its lowest level in about three decades.

Indian markets fell sharply that day, with companies that had big British businesses, such as the Tata group's carmaker and steel arms, taking the brunt. Within weeks the Nifty had recovered and moved on, because nothing about India's own economy had changed.
history.lesson: Political shocks in rich countries tend to fade quickly in India unless they change global growth or money flows.

history.title: The year Germany's gas ran out of cheap
history.story:
After the invasion of Ukraine, Russia steadily reduced gas flows to Europe, and in September 2022 explosions ruptured the Nord Stream pipelines under the Baltic Sea. European gas prices spiked to records. Governments rationed, factories cut output, and households were asked to turn down the heating.

Early in 2023 BASF announced closures and job cuts at its home site in Ludwigshafen, blaming energy costs. The idea that German industry could run on cheap Russian gas was over, and Indian chemical exporters found European rivals at a lasting cost disadvantage.
history.lesson: Dear European energy is a tailwind for Indian chemicals, but only for as long as the gap lasts.

history.title: The Monday the carry trade broke
history.story:
At the end of July 2024, the Bank of Japan raised rates and Governor Kazuo Ueda sounded ready to do more. Days later a weak US jobs report raised hopes of American rate cuts. The gap that made the yen trade work was closing from both ends. The yen soared, and on the first Monday of August Tokyo's Nikkei had its worst day since 1987. Markets from Seoul to Mumbai to New York sold off and volatility gauges spiked.

Two days later Deputy Governor Shinichi Uchida said the bank would not raise rates when markets were unstable. The Nikkei had already bounced the day before. Within a few weeks the Nifty had recovered its losses.
history.lesson: Carry unwinds are violent and brief. Treat them as liquidity events, not as news about India.

today:
India's VIX is at [[val:vix]], which is calm given the size of the oil shock, with Brent at [[val:brent]] a barrel and foreign investors net sellers of [[val:fii20]] over the past twenty sessions. Calm volatility alongside heavy foreign selling means domestic buyers are absorbing the flow; it also means insurance is cheap if a shock from Tokyo arrives.

Both central banks in this chapter have turned. The Bank of Japan raised rates in June 2026 to their highest in about three decades, and Japanese bond yields are at multi-decade highs. The ECB raised rates the same month for the first time since 2023 because of energy-driven inflation. In Europe the carbon border tax is now accruing on every tonne of Indian steel shipped this year, with the first certificates to be bought in early 2027.

Watch next: the yen and Japanese ten-year yields around each Bank of Japan meeting, especially if US data softens at the same time; whether the ECB hikes again; European gas prices while Hormuz stays disrupted; and early CBAM declarations from Indian steel and aluminium exporters.
sowhat:
Japan and Europe matter to Indian portfolios in different ways, so treat them differently.

  • Treat yen-driven sell-offs as liquidity events. When the VIX jumps on a Japanese trigger with no change in Indian fundamentals, history says the damage tends to be repaired within weeks. Indian large caps that foreign funds own heavily fall most and often bounce first.
  • Prefer Indian chemical and pharmaceutical ingredient exporters with European customers while European energy stays dear, keeping an eye on Chinese price competition.
  • Be careful with high-emission steel and aluminium exporters with large European sales. CBAM is a permanent cost, and small mills without emissions data are most exposed.
  • IT services with heavy European exposure feel ECB tightening and European slowdowns through slower deal flow, a few quarters later.
  • Engineering and defence suppliers have a slow, multi-year tailwind from German infrastructure and defence spending.

What would flip it: a sudden Bank of Japan surprise combined with a US slowdown could turn a brief unwind into something longer. A collapse in European gas prices would erode the edge Indian chemicals enjoy, and a real CBAM concession for India in the trade deal's follow-up talks would lift a weight off Indian metals.
